newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Maverick politician may hold key to Bulgarian poll.
newsitem.headline: Maverick politician may hold key to Bulgarian poll.

text.p: Bulgaria's most colourful politician George Ganchev may hold the balance of power in Sunday's presidential elections, if as expected the vote goes to a second round.

Figures from the Laboratory for Political Behaviour showed 32.5 percent support for opposition candidate Petar Stoyanov, 21.5 percent for the Socialist candidate, Culture Minister Ivan Marazov, and Ganchev close behind with 18.5 percent.
Another 16 percent of the 1,570 people polled had not yet decided how they will vote.

"If Ganchev goes through to a second round he may very possibly win," political analyst Miroslav Sevlievski told Reuters. He said if Marazov was eliminated, many Socialist supporters would transfer their votes to Ganchev rather than vote for the candidate of the united opposition.
If the second round is between Stoyanov and Marazov, then the votes of Ganchev's supporters will be key.
Ganchev and his Bulgarian Business Bloc (BBB) have traditionally attracted protest votes from people disillusioned with the two main parties.
A former emigre who spent many years in the United States and formerly held U.S. citizenship, he describes himself as a centrist but his party usually votes with the Socialists in parliament.
The clownish, mustachioed Ganchev, 57, represents a glamorous alternative for an electorate weighed down by falling living standards and disillusioned by bickering politicians.
He is fond of far-fetched tales of his past as a fencing teacher and Hollywood screenwriter, and promises that his famous friends can be called upon to help Bulgaria out of its economic crisis.
Many Bulgarians dismiss him as a buffoon. Prominent sculptor Vezhdi Rashidov told Friday's Troud daily he too would leave the country if Ganchev won.
"How can I live in a state which is on the verge of electing a president who is a petty thief, an absolute liar and a crook like George Ganchev?" he said.

However, Ganchev's simple, direct speaking style appeals to many voters who say he is the only one talking sense, though others are concerned about what could lie behind his "Bulgaria for the Bulgarians" nationalist rhetoric.

He gives voice to many Bulgarians' fears that foreign investors are buying up their country at bargain prices, while at the same time promising to bring in investment from his wealthy foreign business contacts.
Election posters show the imposing two-metre (six foot six inch) former athlete in statesmanlike pose and say simply "George President."

Ganchev won 17 percent of the vote in the 1992 presidential election and his party took 13 of parliament's 240 seats in the 1994 general election, after a campaign enlivened by Ganchev's guitar-playing and public discussion of his love life.
He lost his seat in April 1995 when the Constitutional Court ruled that he had entered parliament illegally because he had held U.S. citizenship at the time of his election.
Under the Bulgarian constitution people with dual citizenship cannot take part in national elections. Three other BBB deputies have since quit the party to become independents.
If there is a second round after Sunday's poll, it will be on November 3.
